source.name: MIT OpenCourseWare 3.091 Introduction to Solid-State Chemistry / Materials Science

course.title: Materials Science
course.description: Why a paperclip bends but a ceramic mug shatters, why copper carries current and diamond does not, and how engineers pick the right material for the job. Bonding and crystal structure, the four classes of materials, phase diagrams, mechanical and electrical behavior, and materials selection. Structure adapted from MIT OpenCourseWare 3.091 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: The type of bonding that holds a block of solid copper together is best described as...
options: metallic, a shared sea of electrons
questions.explanation: Metals share delocalized valence electrons among positive ion cores - see 'Atomic bonding and structure'.

questions.prompt: A crystalline solid differs from an amorphous one because its atoms are...
options: arranged in a repeating, ordered pattern
questions.explanation: Crystals have long-range periodic order; glasses and many polymers are amorphous.

questions.prompt: When you pull on a metal rod and it returns to its original length after release, that behavior is called...
questions.explanation: Elastic strain is fully recoverable; plastic strain is permanent - see 'Mechanical properties'.

questions.prompt: Rubber, nylon, and polyethylene are examples of which class of materials?
questions.explanation: Polymers are long chains of repeating molecular units.

questions.prompt: A material that conducts electricity better than an insulator but worse than a metal, and whose conductivity rises with added impurities, is a...
questions.explanation: Silicon is the classic semiconductor - see 'Semiconductors'.

questions.prompt: The stiffness of a material in the elastic region is measured by its...
questions.explanation: Young's modulus E is the slope of the stress-strain line in the elastic region.

questions.prompt: Ceramics such as alumina tend to be...
questions.explanation: Strong ionic and covalent bonds make ceramics hard and brittle with high melting points.

questions.prompt: A phase diagram tells you, for a given composition and temperature, which...
options: price the metal will sell for
questions.explanation: Phase diagrams map temperature and composition to the stable phases - see 'Phase diagrams'.

lessons.title: Atomic bonding and structure
lessons.grammar_note: Bond type is a spectrum, not a set of boxes - many real materials are partly ionic and partly covalent, and we describe them by the dominant character.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the four primary bonding types and predict, from bonding, whether a material will be hard, conductive, or brittle. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what kind of bond holds solid copper together, and what does that bond let the electrons do?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Every property of a solid traces back to how its atoms are held together. In ionic bonding, one atom donates electrons and another accepts them, and the resulting positive and negative ions attract - as in table salt, NaCl. In covalent bonding, atoms share electron pairs directionally, as in diamond, giving very hard, often insulating solids. In metallic bonding, atoms release their valence electrons into a shared 'sea' that flows freely, which is why metals conduct electricity and heat and can be bent without shattering. Weak van der Waals and hydrogen bonds act between molecules; they are what hold polymer chains loosely to one another. Stronger bonds generally mean higher melting points and greater stiffness.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Sodium chloride (NaCl): a sodium atom gives up one electron to chlorine, forming Na+ and Cl- ions in a rigid lattice - high melting point (801 C), brittle, and an insulator when solid. Diamond: each carbon shares four covalent bonds in a rigid 3D network - the hardest natural material, and an electrical insulator despite being pure carbon. Copper: a lattice of Cu+ cores in a sea of mobile electrons - soft enough to draw into wire, and an excellent conductor. Polyethylene: strong covalent bonds run along each carbon chain, but only weak van der Waals forces hold neighboring chains together, so it melts at low temperature and is easily deformed.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which bond type gives a shared sea of mobile electrons? 2) Predict whether an ionic solid like NaCl conducts electricity as a dry solid. 3) Diamond and copper are both made of one element type each; why is diamond an insulator and copper a conductor? 4) Which is stronger, a covalent bond within a polymer chain or the van der Waals force between chains? 5) Would you expect a material with strong bonds to have a high or low melting point? Answers: 1) Metallic bonding. 2) No - its electrons are locked in ions, so solid NaCl is an insulator (it conducts only when molten or dissolved). 3) Diamond's electrons are all locked in fixed covalent bonds; copper's valence electrons roam freely. 4) The covalent bond along the chain is far stronger. 5) High.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming any material made of a metal element must conduct - a metal oxide like rust is a poor conductor because its electrons are tied up in ionic bonds. Mistake: treating bond types as strict boxes when most real bonds are mixed in character. Exit: (a) Which bonding type explains why metals bend rather than shatter? (b) Name one property that generally rises as bond strength rises. Answers: metallic bonding, whose electron sea lets atomic planes slide; melting point (or stiffness/hardness).

lessons.title: Crystal structures and defects
lessons.grammar_note: A defect is not a flaw to be ashamed of - controlled defects are how engineers tune strength, color, and conductivity on purpose.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the common cubic crystal structures, compute a simple packing count, and classify defects by dimension. Warm-up: what is the difference between a crystalline solid and an amorphous one?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: In a crystal, atoms sit at the points of a repeating lattice. Three common metal arrangements are simple cubic, body-centered cubic (BCC, an atom at each corner plus one in the center), and face-centered cubic (FCC, corners plus one on each face). FCC and hexagonal close-packed (HCP) achieve the densest packing, filling about 74 percent of space. Real crystals are never perfect. Point defects are zero-dimensional: a vacancy is a missing atom, and a substitutional or interstitial impurity is a foreign atom in or between lattice sites. Line defects, called dislocations, are one-dimensional and are the key to how metals deform. Planar defects like grain boundaries are two-dimensional surfaces where crystal orientation changes. Defects are not merely damage: adding carbon atoms to iron to make steel, or dopant atoms to silicon, deliberately uses point defects to control properties.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Counting atoms in a BCC unit cell: each of the 8 corner atoms is shared among 8 neighboring cells, contributing 8 x 1/8 = 1 atom, plus the 1 full atom in the center, for 2 atoms per cell. For FCC: 8 corners x 1/8 = 1, plus 6 faces x 1/2 = 3, giving 4 atoms per cell. Packing efficiency: FCC and HCP both fill about 74 percent of space, BCC about 68 percent, and simple cubic only about 52 percent. Defect in action: dissolving about 0.2 percent carbon into iron pins its dislocations and turns soft iron into much harder steel.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) How many atoms belong to a single FCC unit cell? 2) A corner atom in a cubic cell is shared among how many cells? 3) Which packs more densely, BCC or FCC? 4) A missing atom in the lattice is which kind of defect? 5) What dimension is a grain boundary? 6) Name one property engineers tune by adding impurity atoms. Answers: 1) 4 atoms. 2) 8 cells, so it contributes 1/8. 3) FCC, about 74 percent versus about 68 percent. 4) A vacancy, which is a point (zero-dimensional) defect. 5) Two-dimensional (a planar defect). 6) Strength (steel), or electrical conductivity (doped silicon), or color.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: counting every corner atom as a whole atom instead of 1/8, which overcounts the unit cell. Mistake: thinking a perfect crystal is always the goal, when controlled defects are often the point. Exit: (a) How many atoms are in a BCC unit cell? (b) Dislocations are defects of what dimension? Answers: 2 atoms; one-dimensional (line) defects.

lessons.title: The four classes of materials
lessons.grammar_note: Composite is the odd one out: it is defined by combining two of the other classes, not by a single bonding type.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Sort a material into metals, ceramics, polymers, or composites, and connect each class to its typical bonding and properties. Warm-up: which class do rubber and nylon belong to, and what are their molecules shaped like?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Engineering materials fall into four broad families. Metals (steel, aluminum, copper) are held by metallic bonds; they are dense, conductive, ductile, and strong. Ceramics (alumina, silica, brick) are held by ionic and covalent bonds; they are hard, brittle, chemically stable, and resist heat, but crack rather than bend. Polymers (polyethylene, nylon, rubber) are long chains of repeating units held to one another by weak forces; they are light, flexible, cheap, and easy to shape, but soften with heat. Composites (fiberglass, carbon-fiber, reinforced concrete) combine two of the above to get the best of each: stiff, strong fibers embedded in a tough matrix. Choosing among classes is a trade-off among strength, weight, cost, and how the material fails.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: A steel beam: metallic bonding gives high strength and the ability to bend before breaking, so it warns you before it fails. A ceramic mug: strong rigid bonds make it hard and heat-resistant, but with no way to relieve stress it shatters when dropped. A plastic bottle (polymer): light and easily molded, but it deforms in hot water. Fiberglass (composite): brittle glass fibers give stiffness while a flexible resin matrix holds them together and stops cracks from running, so the pair is tougher than either alone. Reinforced concrete pairs concrete (strong in compression) with steel bars (strong in tension).

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which class is defined by combining two others? 2) Why does a ceramic mug shatter while a metal spoon bends? 3) Rubber belongs to which class? 4) Which class is generally the lightest and cheapest to shape? 5) In fiberglass, which part carries the load and which holds it together? 6) Which class best resists high temperature and chemical attack? Answers: 1) Composites. 2) The ceramic's rigid bonds cannot slide to relieve stress, so it fractures; the metal's electron sea lets planes slip and deform. 3) Polymers. 4) Polymers. 5) The glass fibers carry the load; the resin matrix binds and protects them. 6) Ceramics.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling every hard material a metal - many hard materials (diamond, alumina) are ceramics. Mistake: assuming a composite is just a mixture; the point is that each phase does a distinct job. Exit: (a) Name the four classes. (b) Which class is brittle and heat-resistant? Answers: metals, ceramics, polymers, composites; ceramics.

questions.prompt: The mobile 'sea of electrons' that explains a metal's conductivity comes from which bonding type?
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding delocalizes valence electrons across the lattice.

questions.prompt: A body-centered cubic (BCC) unit cell contains how many atoms in total?
questions.explanation: 8 corners x 1/8 = 1, plus 1 center atom, equals 2 atoms.

questions.prompt: A vacancy in a crystal lattice is an example of a...
questions.explanation: A missing atom is a zero-dimensional point defect.

questions.prompt: Which class of materials is defined by combining two of the other classes?
questions.explanation: Composites join, for example, stiff fibers with a tough matrix.

questions.prompt: Alumina (a ceramic) is best described as...
questions.explanation: Strong ionic and covalent bonds make ceramics hard, brittle, and heat-resistant.

questions.prompt: Face-centered cubic (FCC) packing fills roughly what fraction of space?
questions.explanation: FCC and HCP are close-packed at about 74 percent.

lessons.title: Phase diagrams
lessons.grammar_note: Read a phase diagram like a map: the horizontal axis is composition, the vertical axis is temperature, and every point tells you which phases are stable there.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a binary phase diagram, identify single- and two-phase regions, and use the lever rule to find how much of each phase is present. Warm-up: what two quantities does a phase diagram plot on its axes?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A phase is a region of uniform structure and composition, like solid, liquid, or a particular crystal. A binary phase diagram plots temperature (vertical) against composition of a two-element mixture (horizontal) and shades in which phases are stable at each point. The liquidus line marks where a melt begins to freeze; the solidus marks where it is fully solid. Between them lies a two-phase region where solid and liquid coexist. A special composition called the eutectic melts at a single low temperature, lower than either pure component. When you land in a two-phase region, the lever rule gives the fraction of each phase: draw a horizontal tie-line, and the fraction of one phase equals the length of the opposite arm divided by the whole tie-line length.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Lever rule: suppose at some temperature the solid phase sits at 20 percent B, the liquid at 60 percent B, and your overall alloy is at 30 percent B. The total tie-line length is 60 - 20 = 40. The fraction of liquid equals the arm from the solid to the overall point divided by the total: (30 - 20) / 40 = 10/40 = 0.25, so 25 percent liquid. The fraction of solid is the opposite arm: (60 - 30) / 40 = 30/40 = 0.75, so 75 percent solid. Note the fractions add to 1. Eutectic idea: the lead-tin solder system has a eutectic that melts at about 183 C, well below pure lead (327 C) or pure tin (232 C), which is exactly why that mix flows so easily for soldering.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which axis of a binary phase diagram is composition? 2) What does the liquidus line mark? 3) An alloy at 40 percent B lies in a two-phase region with solid at 30 percent B and liquid at 70 percent B. What fraction is liquid? 4) In the same case, what fraction is solid? 5) Why does a eutectic composition matter for soldering? Answers: 1) The horizontal axis. 2) The temperature at which a cooling liquid first begins to solidify. 3) Liquid fraction = (40 - 30) / (70 - 30) = 10/40 = 0.25, so 25 percent. 4) Solid fraction = (70 - 40) / 40 = 30/40 = 0.75, so 75 percent. 5) It melts at the lowest temperature of the system, so the solder flows and sets easily.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using the near arm instead of the far arm - the fraction of a phase uses the length of the tie-line arm on the opposite side of the overall composition. Mistake: forgetting that the two phase fractions must sum to 1. Exit: (a) What are the two axes of a binary phase diagram? (b) At an overall 25 percent B with solid at 15 and liquid at 55, what fraction is solid? Answers: temperature and composition; solid fraction = (55 - 25) / (55 - 15) = 30/40 = 0.75, so 75 percent.

lessons.title: Mechanical properties: stress, strain, elasticity, plasticity
lessons.grammar_note: Stress is force per unit area (how hard you push), while strain is the fractional change in length (how much it stretches) - keep the two straight.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define stress and strain, read a stress-strain curve, and tell elastic from plastic behavior. Warm-up: if a rod stretches under load and springs fully back when released, is that elastic or plastic?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Stress is force divided by cross-sectional area, in units of pascals (Pa = N/m^2). Strain is the change in length divided by the original length, a dimensionless ratio. Plotting stress against strain reveals a material's mechanical character. At first the curve is a straight line: this is the elastic region, where deformation is fully recovered on unloading, and the slope is Young's modulus E (Hooke's law: stress = E x strain). Past the yield strength the material deforms plastically, meaning permanently. The curve rises to a peak, the ultimate tensile strength, then falls until fracture. A ductile material shows a long plastic region and stretches a lot before breaking; a brittle material snaps soon after the elastic region with little warning.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Stress: a 1000 N load on a rod of cross-section 0.0001 m^2 gives stress = 1000 / 0.0001 = 10,000,000 Pa = 10 MPa. Strain: a 2.00 m bar that stretches by 2 mm has strain = 0.002 / 2.00 = 0.001, or 0.1 percent. Young's modulus from Hooke's law: if 200 MPa of stress produces 0.001 strain in the elastic region, then E = stress / strain = 200 MPa / 0.001 = 200,000 MPa = 200 GPa, about right for steel. Ductile versus brittle: mild steel yields and stretches noticeably before breaking, giving warning; glass stays elastic right up to a sudden fracture.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) A 500 N force acts on an area of 0.0005 m^2. What is the stress? 2) A 4 m cable stretches 8 mm. What is the strain? 3) Which region of the stress-strain curve is fully recoverable? 4) What does the slope of the elastic region measure? 5) If a stress of 100 MPa gives a strain of 0.0005 in the elastic region, what is E? 6) Which fails with more warning, a ductile or a brittle material? Answers: 1) 500 / 0.0005 = 1,000,000 Pa = 1 MPa. 2) 0.008 / 4 = 0.002, or 0.2 percent. 3) The elastic region. 4) Young's modulus (stiffness). 5) E = 100 MPa / 0.0005 = 200,000 MPa = 200 GPa. 6) Ductile - it deforms visibly first.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing stiffness (Young's modulus) with strength (the stress a material can bear before yielding or breaking) - a material can be stiff yet weak, or strong yet flexible. Mistake: forgetting that strain is dimensionless. Exit: (a) Which point on the curve marks the start of permanent deformation? (b) What is stress = E x strain called? Answers: the yield strength; Hooke's law.

lessons.title: Failure and fatigue
lessons.grammar_note: Fatigue is failure by repetition, not by overload - the peak stress each cycle can sit well below the strength that a single steady pull would need.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish ductile from brittle fracture, explain fatigue and stress concentration, and describe why cracks matter. Warm-up: from the last lesson, which fails with less warning, a ductile or a brittle material?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Materials fail in more than one way. Ductile fracture is preceded by visible plastic stretching and necking, giving warning. Brittle fracture is sudden, with a crack racing through the material at almost no plastic deformation. Sharp corners, notches, and existing cracks act as stress concentrators: the local stress at a crack tip can be many times the average applied stress, which is why a tiny scratch can start a big failure. Fatigue is failure under repeated cyclic loading at stresses well below the single-load strength; each cycle grows a crack a little until the remaining section can no longer hold. Creep is slow, permanent deformation under a steady load at high temperature over long times. Toughness is the energy a material absorbs before fracturing, combining strength and ductility.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Stress concentration: a small elliptical flaw can raise the local stress at its tip to several times the applied stress, so a plate that is safe on average can still fail from one sharp scratch. Fatigue: an aircraft component cycled millions of times can crack and fail at a peak stress far below its rated tensile strength; this is why safety-critical parts are inspected and retired on a schedule rather than run to visible damage. Ductile versus brittle in practice: a steel paperclip bends and necks before it breaks (ductile), while a glass rod snaps clean with no warning (brittle). Toughness: adding a rubbery phase to a brittle plastic raises the energy it absorbs before cracking.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which fracture type gives warning through visible stretching? 2) Why does a sharp scratch weaken a part more than a smooth surface? 3) Fatigue failure happens at stresses that are higher or lower than the single-pull strength? 4) What is creep? 5) What property measures the energy absorbed before fracture? 6) Why are aircraft parts retired on a schedule? Answers: 1) Ductile fracture. 2) The scratch concentrates stress at its tip, multiplying the local stress far above the average. 3) Lower - many small cycles do the damage. 4) Slow permanent deformation under a steady load at high temperature over long times. 5) Toughness. 6) Because fatigue cracks grow invisibly with each cycle until failure, so parts are replaced before that point.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a part is safe just because a single load never exceeds its strength - cyclic loading can fail it by fatigue far below that level. Mistake: treating strength and toughness as the same thing; a very strong but brittle material can have low toughness. Exit: (a) What kind of loading causes fatigue? (b) What do sharp corners and cracks do to local stress? Answers: repeated cyclic loading; they concentrate (multiply) the local stress.

questions.prompt: On a binary phase diagram, the horizontal axis represents...
questions.explanation: Composition runs horizontally; temperature runs vertically.

questions.prompt: In a two-phase region with solid at 20 percent B, liquid at 60 percent B, and overall alloy at 30 percent B, the fraction of solid is...
questions.explanation: Solid fraction = (60 - 30) / (60 - 20) = 30/40 = 0.75 by the lever rule.

questions.prompt: The slope of the straight elastic portion of a stress-strain curve is the...
questions.explanation: Stress = E x strain (Hooke's law), so the slope is Young's modulus.

questions.prompt: Deformation that is permanent and not recovered on unloading is...
questions.explanation: Plastic deformation is permanent; elastic deformation springs back.

questions.prompt: Fatigue failure occurs when a material is subjected to...
options: repeated cyclic loading below its single-load strength
questions.explanation: Cyclic stresses grow a crack over many cycles at loads below the tensile strength.

questions.prompt: A eutectic composition is notable because it...
options: melts at the lowest temperature in the system
questions.explanation: The eutectic melts at a single temperature lower than either pure component.

lessons.title: Electrical and thermal properties
lessons.grammar_note: Conductivity and resistivity are reciprocals: high conductivity means low resistivity, so quoting one implies the other.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Rank materials by electrical conductivity, explain why metals conduct heat well, and describe thermal expansion. Warm-up: from the bonding lesson, what feature of metals lets them carry electric current?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Electrical conductivity measures how easily charge flows; resistivity is its reciprocal. Metals conduct well because their sea of free electrons drifts under a voltage. Insulators such as ceramics and most polymers have no free carriers and block current. Semiconductors sit in between and are covered next. Interestingly, in metals the same free electrons that carry charge also carry heat, so good electrical conductors are usually good thermal conductors too (the Wiedemann-Franz relationship). Materials also expand when heated: the thermal expansion coefficient tells how much length grows per degree of temperature rise, which is why bridges need expansion gaps. Heating a metal actually lowers its conductivity, because hotter atoms vibrate more and scatter the moving electrons.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Conductivity ranking: copper and silver conduct best, then aluminum; silicon (a semiconductor) is far lower; glass and most plastics are insulators. Heat and charge together: copper is both an excellent electrical conductor and an excellent thermal conductor, which is why cookware bottoms and heat sinks are often copper or aluminum. Thermal expansion: a steel bridge span 1000 m long with an expansion coefficient near 12 x 10^-6 per degree C grows about 1000 x 12 x 10^-6 x 30 = 0.36 m over a 30 degree C rise, so engineers build in expansion joints. Temperature effect: warming a copper wire raises its resistance because lattice vibrations scatter the electrons more.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Resistivity is the reciprocal of what quantity? 2) Why do metals conduct electricity well? 3) Name a material that is a good electrical insulator. 4) In metals, do good electrical conductors also tend to conduct heat well? 5) Does a metal's conductivity rise or fall as it heats up? 6) Why do long bridges include expansion joints? Answers: 1) Electrical conductivity. 2) Their free (delocalized) electrons drift under an applied voltage. 3) Glass, most ceramics, or most plastics. 4) Yes - the same free electrons carry both. 5) It falls, because vibrating atoms scatter the electrons. 6) The material expands when heated, so gaps prevent buckling.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming heating always increases conductivity - in metals it decreases it, though in semiconductors it increases it. Mistake: confusing conductivity with resistivity, which are reciprocals. Exit: (a) Why are copper and aluminum used for heat sinks? (b) What happens to a metal's electrical resistance as temperature rises? Answers: they conduct heat well (and are affordable); it increases.

lessons.title: Semiconductors
lessons.grammar_note: Doping is deliberate impurity: n-type adds spare electrons (negative carriers), p-type adds holes (positive carriers) - the letter names the sign of the extra charge carrier.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the band gap, distinguish n-type from p-type doping, and describe what a p-n junction does. Warm-up: a semiconductor conducts better than an insulator but worse than a metal - and its conductivity does what when you add impurities?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Whether a material conducts depends on its band gap, the energy jump an electron must make from the filled valence band to the empty conduction band where it can move. Conductors have overlapping bands (no gap), insulators have a large gap, and semiconductors like silicon have a small gap that a little energy can bridge. Doping adds tiny amounts of impurity to control conductivity. n-type doping (for example, phosphorus in silicon) adds atoms with a spare electron, giving negative carriers. p-type doping (for example, boron) adds atoms short one electron, creating positive 'holes' that carry charge. Joining an n-type and a p-type region forms a p-n junction, which lets current pass one way but not the other - the diode, and the foundation of essentially every electronic device.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Band gap sizes: a conductor has effectively zero gap, silicon has a gap of about 1.1 eV, and diamond (an insulator) has a gap near 5.5 eV, which is why silicon conducts modestly and diamond does not. Doping: replacing a few silicon atoms with phosphorus (5 outer electrons versus silicon's 4) leaves a spare electron per dopant, making n-type material; replacing them with boron (3 outer electrons) leaves a hole, making p-type. p-n junction: put the two together and the junction conducts when forward-biased but blocks reverse current, which is exactly the behavior of a diode. Temperature effect: unlike a metal, a semiconductor conducts better when heated, because heat lifts more electrons across the small gap.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the band gap? 2) Does silicon have a larger or smaller band gap than diamond? 3) n-type doping supplies which kind of charge carrier? 4) What carrier does p-type doping create? 5) What does a p-n junction (diode) do to current? 6) When you heat a semiconductor, does its conductivity rise or fall? Answers: 1) The energy an electron must gain to jump from the valence band to the conduction band. 2) Smaller (about 1.1 eV versus about 5.5 eV). 3) Extra (negative) electrons. 4) Positive holes. 5) It lets current flow one way but blocks the other. 6) It rises, because heat promotes more electrons across the gap.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking p-type material is positively charged overall - it is electrically neutral; the 'holes' are just mobile positive-charge carriers. Mistake: assuming more doping always helps, when the goal is precise control, not maximum conductivity. Exit: (a) Which doping type provides extra electrons? (b) Does a semiconductor's conductivity increase or decrease with temperature? Answers: n-type; it increases.

lessons.title: Materials selection
lessons.grammar_note: There is rarely one best material - selection means ranking candidates against the requirements that actually matter for your part.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Turn a design requirement into material properties, compare candidates on a specific-property basis, and reason about cost trade-offs. Warm-up: for a part that must be both strong and light, is raw strength alone the right thing to compare?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Selecting a material means matching what a part must do to the properties that deliver it, then trading off among competing needs and cost. A common goal is high strength for low weight, so engineers compare specific strength, which is strength divided by density, rather than strength alone. Similarly, specific stiffness is Young's modulus divided by density. Other constraints enter: operating temperature (ceramics for heat), electrical needs (copper to conduct, a polymer to insulate), corrosion resistance, how the part fails (ductile warning versus brittle surprise), how it will be manufactured, and always cost. A useful tool is a property chart that plots one property against another so whole families of materials can be compared at a glance.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Specific strength: suppose steel has strength 400 MPa and density 7.8 g/cm^3, giving 400 / 7.8 = 51 (MPa per g/cm^3), while an aluminum alloy at 300 MPa and 2.7 g/cm^3 gives 300 / 2.7 = 111. Even though the steel is stronger in absolute terms, the aluminum carries far more load per unit weight, which is why aircraft favor it. Function to property: a heat sink needs high thermal conductivity plus low cost, pointing to aluminum; a cutting tool needs hardness and heat resistance, pointing to a ceramic or carbide; a drink bottle needs to be light, cheap, and moldable, pointing to a polymer. Cost check: carbon-fiber composite beats aluminum on specific strength but costs far more, so it is chosen only where weight savings justify the price.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is specific strength? 2) Steel at 400 MPa and 7.8 g/cm^3 versus aluminum at 300 MPa and 2.7 g/cm^3 - which has the higher specific strength? 3) What property matters most for a heat sink? 4) Why might an engineer reject carbon fiber even when it performs best? 5) For an electrical insulator in a plug, which material class fits? 6) Name two constraints besides strength that guide selection. Answers: 1) Strength divided by density. 2) Aluminum (111 versus 51). 3) High thermal conductivity (plus low cost). 4) Its cost is too high to justify unless weight savings are critical. 5) A polymer (or ceramic). 6) Any two of: operating temperature, corrosion resistance, cost, manufacturability, failure mode, electrical needs.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: comparing absolute strength when weight matters, instead of specific strength. Mistake: optimizing one property and ignoring cost or manufacturability, which often decide the real choice. Exit: (a) Why do aircraft often prefer aluminum over stronger steel? (b) What does specific stiffness divide Young's modulus by? Answers: aluminum's higher specific strength (strength per weight); density.

questions.prompt: Compared with an insulator, a semiconductor's band gap is...
questions.explanation: Semiconductors have a small nonzero gap; insulators have a large one and conductors effectively none.

questions.prompt: n-type doping of silicon supplies extra...
questions.explanation: n-type dopants like phosphorus donate spare electrons.

questions.prompt: As a metal is heated, its electrical conductivity generally...
questions.explanation: Hotter atoms vibrate and scatter electrons more, lowering conductivity (opposite to a semiconductor).

questions.prompt: For a strong yet lightweight part, engineers compare candidates by their...
questions.explanation: Specific strength captures load-bearing capacity per unit weight.

questions.prompt: A p-n junction is useful because it...
options: lets current pass in one direction but not the other
questions.explanation: That one-way behavior is exactly what a diode does.

questions.prompt: The same free electrons in a metal that carry electric charge also largely carry...
questions.explanation: This is why good electrical conductors are usually good thermal conductors.

lessons.title: Capstone: choose a material for a bicycle frame
lessons.grammar_note: A good selection argument names the requirements first, then shows how each candidate meets or fails them - the winner is justified, not just asserted.

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: You must recommend a material for a bicycle frame. It has to be strong enough to carry a rider safely, as light as possible for easy riding, resistant to corrosion from rain and sweat, affordable for a mid-range bike, and able to warn of failure rather than snap without notice. Work through the four material classes, apply what this course covered, and defend a single recommendation. Do not just name a material; build the argument.

sections.heading: The requirements, made concrete
sections.text: Translate each need into a property from earlier lessons. 'Strong but light' means high specific strength (strength divided by density), not just absolute strength. 'Warns before failing' means favor a ductile material over a brittle one, from the failure-and-fatigue lesson. 'Survives rain and sweat' means good corrosion resistance. 'Affordable' means moderate material and manufacturing cost. 'Lasts through years of pedaling' means good fatigue resistance under millions of load cycles. List these five requirements before comparing anything.

sections.heading: Weigh the four classes
sections.text: Ceramics: very hard and stiff but brittle, so they fail suddenly with no warning - reject for a load-bearing frame. Polymers alone: light and cheap but too flexible and weak for the loads and stresses of a frame - reject on strength. Metals: steel is strong, ductile, cheap, and fails with warning, but it is dense (heavy) and can rust without protection; aluminum alloy has a higher specific strength, resists corrosion with its natural oxide layer, and is moderate in cost, though it is less fatigue-tolerant and must be designed with thicker tubes. Composites: carbon-fiber gives the best specific strength of all and does not corrode, but it costs the most and can fail in a brittle way if damaged.

sections.heading: A worked recommendation
sections.text: For a mid-range bike, aluminum alloy is the strongest all-around choice. It beats steel on specific strength (recall aluminum's roughly 111 versus steel's 51 in the selection lesson), so the frame is lighter for the same load. Its oxide layer handles rain and sweat, meeting the corrosion requirement. Its cost sits between cheap steel and expensive carbon fiber, meeting the budget. Its main weakness, lower fatigue resistance, is managed by using larger-diameter, thicker-walled tubes so each cycle sees lower stress. Steel would be the pick if lowest cost and easy repair mattered most; carbon fiber would win for a high-end racing frame where weight justifies the price. This kind of reasoning - requirements first, candidates judged against them, a justified winner and the runner-up conditions - is exactly how materials selection is done.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: Check yes to each: you listed the five requirements before comparing materials; you translated 'strong but light' into specific strength rather than absolute strength; you rejected ceramics and standalone polymers for concrete reasons (brittleness, insufficient strength); you compared metals and composites on specific strength, corrosion, cost, and failure mode; and you named a single recommendation with the trade-off that would change it. If all five hold, you have made a sound materials-selection argument.

questions.prompt: A metal bends rather than shatters mainly because...
options: its sea of electrons lets atomic planes slide
questions.explanation: Metallic bonding allows planes to slip past one another, giving ductility.

questions.prompt: An FCC unit cell contains how many atoms?
questions.explanation: 8 corners x 1/8 = 1 plus 6 faces x 1/2 = 3, giving 4 atoms.

questions.prompt: Which class of materials is hard, brittle, and heat-resistant?
questions.explanation: Strong ionic and covalent bonds make ceramics hard, brittle, and heat-resistant.

questions.prompt: In a two-phase region, the lever rule computes the...
questions.explanation: The tie-line arms give the fraction of each coexisting phase.

questions.prompt: The yield strength on a stress-strain curve marks the onset of...
questions.explanation: Beyond yield, deformation is no longer fully recovered.

questions.prompt: Fatigue causes failure when a part is...
options: loaded repeatedly below its single-load strength
kept at constant load forever with no motion
questions.explanation: Repeated cycles grow a crack until the section fails, at stresses below the tensile strength.

questions.prompt: p-type doping of silicon creates charge carriers that are...
questions.explanation: p-type dopants like boron leave positive holes that carry charge.

questions.prompt: For a strong, lightweight bicycle frame, the best single comparison metric is...
questions.explanation: Specific strength captures load capacity per unit weight, the key for light structures.
